title: Interleave Two Sequences, Lazily
statement:
`yield return` turns a method into a state machine the compiler writes for
you: each call to the resulting sequence's `MoveNext()` runs the method
body until the next `yield return`, then pauses there -- mid-loop, mid
whatever it was doing -- until asked to resume. Writing an iterator that
pulls from *two* sequences at once means managing that pause point by
hand, one `IEnumerator<T>` per source, because nothing hands you both
sequences' current positions in a single `foreach`.

## Your function

```
public static IEnumerable<int> Interleave(IEnumerable<int> a, IEnumerable<int> b);
```

Yield elements alternately from `a` and `b`: `a`'s first element, then
`b`'s first, then `a`'s second, then `b`'s second, and so on. Once one
sequence is exhausted, yield the remainder of the other one in order --
do not stop early, and do not pad the exhausted side with anything.
Either sequence may be empty.

## Watch out

- **`GetEnumerator()` and `MoveNext()`, not `foreach`.** A `foreach` loop
  owns its enumerator for its entire body and cannot be paused
  mid-iteration to let the *other* sequence take a turn -- interleaving
  two sequences means holding one `IEnumerator<int>` per source yourself,
  calling `MoveNext()` on each in turn, and reading `.Current` only when
  the matching `MoveNext()` just returned `true`.
- **Once a sequence is exhausted, stop asking it for more, but keep
  asking the other one.** A loop that keeps trying to advance a
  finished enumerator does no harm (`MoveNext()` on an exhausted
  enumerator just keeps returning `false`), but a loop that stops the
  *whole* interleave the moment either side finishes drops every
  remaining element of the longer sequence -- exactly what "yield the
  remainder" rules out.
- `IEnumerator<T>` implements `IDisposable`; wrap each one in a `using`
  (or a `using` declaration) so it is disposed whether the interleave
  runs to completion or a caller stops enumerating partway through.
